terms.title: Red Teaming
terms.passage:
Deliberately attacking your own LLM system to find safety, security and misuse failures before real users or attackers do.

Red teaming is the practice of trying to break your own AI system on purpose. A red team, whether internal staff, outside specialists or automated attack generators, plays the adversary: they attempt jailbreaks, prompt injection, data extraction, policy violations and misuse of tools, then report what worked so it can be fixed. It is the security mindset applied to model behavior. The value shows up in what it catches before launch. A bank preparing to release an account assistant agent ran a two week red team exercise. Testers discovered that by asking the agent to "summarize my recent activity including any linked accounts", they could get it to reveal transactions from a spouse's joint account the user was not authorized to see. The bug was in tool permissions, not the model, but only adversarial use revealed it. A useful red team exercise usually covers several areas: Area Example question Safety Can it be made to produce harmful instructions? Security Can injected content trigger tool calls or leak data? Privacy Can it reveal other users' data or its own system prompt? Policy Will it make commitments, give legal advice, or go off brand? Abuse Can it be used at scale for spam or fraud? Manual and automated approaches complement each other. Human testers are creative and find novel multi step attacks.

terms.title: Regression Evals
terms.passage:
Evals run automatically on every change to catch cases where something that used to work stops working.

Regression evals are evals that run automatically whenever the system changes, with the specific job of catching anything that used to work and no longer does. They are the LLM equivalent of a regression test suite in CI: less about measuring overall quality and more about guarding what you have already fixed. The need is driven by how changes interact in LLM systems. A small edit meant to fix one behavior often breaks another. One team added a line to the system prompt telling the model to be concise; it fixed rambling answers and also caused the model to drop the safety disclaimer required on medical questions. Nobody noticed for two weeks because nobody was looking at medical questions when they tested conciseness. A regression suite is built from cases you already care about. It typically draws from a golden dataset, with priority given to past bugs, compliance critical behaviors and high traffic intents. Each case needs a clear pass or fail condition, scored by code where possible and by an LLM as judge where not. terms.title: Reranking
terms.passage:
A second retrieval pass where a slower, more accurate model reorders candidate documents by how well they answer the query.

Reranking is a second pass over retrieved candidates in which a more precise model scores each one against the query and reorders the list. The first stage retriever is built for speed across millions of documents; the reranker is built for accuracy across a few dozen. The symptom that leads teams to add a reranker is usually "the right document was retrieved but not used." Logs show the correct chunk sitting at position 14, while only the top 5 make it into the prompt. Fast retrievers compare a query embedding with document embeddings computed independently, so they cannot weigh how specific words in the question relate to specific words in the passage. A reranker, usually a cross encoder or a small LLM, reads the query and each candidate together and catches those relationships. The standard shape is retrieve wide, rerank narrow. Pull 50 to 100 candidates using hybrid search, rerank them, and pass the best 5 to 10 to the model. This lets the cheap step optimize for recall and the expensive step optimize for precision. terms.title: Retries and Timeouts
terms.passage:
Rules for how long to wait on a model call and when to try again, so slow or failed requests don't hang or cascade.

Retries and timeouts decide what your application does when a model call is slow or fails. A timeout sets the maximum time you will wait before giving up; a retry policy decides which failures are worth trying again, how many times, and with what delay. LLM calls fail more often and vary in duration more than typical API calls, so these settings matter more than usual. The default settings are often the problem. One team's chat endpoint had an HTTP client timeout of ten minutes inherited from a library default. When the provider degraded, requests piled up, worker threads were exhausted, and the whole web app stopped responding, including pages that never called the model. A 30 second timeout and a small worker pool for LLM calls would have contained the damage to one feature. Choosing a timeout for generation is tricky because duration depends on output length. A request that produces 2,000 tokens legitimately takes much longer than one that produces 50. With streaming, it helps to use two limits: a short timeout on time to first token, which catches stuck requests quickly, and a longer overall limit for the full response. terms.title: Retrieval Metrics
terms.passage:
Scores such as recall@k, MRR and nDCG that measure whether retrieval returns the right documents near the top.

Retrieval metrics measure the search half of a RAG system on its own, separate from what the model writes. You need a set of queries where you know which documents or chunks are relevant, then you run retrieval and score how many of them came back and how high they ranked. The most useful metric is usually recall@k: the share of relevant items that appear in the top k results, where k is the number of chunks you actually put in the prompt. If the answer needs one chunk and it sits at position 12 while you send the top 5, the model never sees it. Precision@k, the share of the top k that is relevant, matters when irrelevant chunks distract the model or waste tokens. Ranking aware metrics tell you whether the good results come first. terms.title: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)
terms.passage:
Training a model with human preference judgments so its answers become more helpful, safer, and closer to what people want.

RLHF is a training stage that shapes a model's behavior using human judgments of which answers are better. After a model is pretrained and given basic instruction tuning through supervised fine tuning, people compare pairs of its responses and pick the preferred one. Those preferences train a reward model, and the LLM is then optimized to produce responses that the reward model scores highly. Newer methods such as direct preference optimization skip the separate reward model but rely on the same kind of preference data. Most application engineers never run RLHF themselves, but they live with its effects every day. The tendency of a chat model to be polite, to hedge, to refuse certain requests, and to format answers with headings and bullet points all come largely from preference training. When a team found their customer facing bot adding cheerful apologies to error messages that should have been terse, the cause was not their system prompt but trained in preferences they had to explicitly override. Preference training also explains some failure modes. Reward models can favor answers that sound confident and thorough over answers that are correct, which nudges models toward plausible hallucination rather than admitting uncertainty. It can produce sycophancy, where the model agrees with a user's wrong claim because agreement was rated well. Knowing this helps when writing

terms.title: Semantic Caching
terms.passage:
Reusing a stored LLM response when a new query means roughly the same thing as an earlier one, judged by embedding similarity.

Semantic caching serves a previously generated answer when a new request is close in meaning to one already seen, even if the wording differs. Instead of keying the cache on the exact prompt text, you compute an embedding of the query, run a similarity search against embeddings of past queries, and if the closest match is above a similarity threshold, return its stored response without calling the model. The appeal is the hit rate. Exact match caching rarely helps with natural language because users phrase the same question in endless ways: "how do I reset my password", "forgot password help", "can't log in, need new password". A semantic cache can treat these as one question. A software company's help bot saw its hit rate climb from about three percent with exact matching to around thirty five percent with semantic matching, cutting both model spend and median latency on those requests. The danger is that "similar" is not the same as "equivalent". The same help bot later served the answer for "how do I delete my account" to someone who asked "how do I delete my team account", which involved a different and far more destructive process. The embeddings were close; the correct answers were not. Small words such as "not", "team", "before" and product names can flip the meaning while

terms.title: Similarity Search
terms.passage:
Finding the stored items whose vectors are closest to a query vector, used to retrieve content by meaning rather than keywords.

Similarity search is the process of finding the items in a collection that are most similar to a query, measured by the distance between their vectors. You turn the query into an embedding, compare it against stored embeddings using a measure such as cosine similarity or dot product, and return the top k closest results. It is how a RAG system finds passages relevant to a question that may not share any exact words with them. Exact search compares the query with every stored vector, which is accurate but slow once you have millions of items. Production systems almost always use approximate nearest neighbor indexes, such as HNSW or IVF, that trade a little accuracy for large speed gains. A vector database manages these indexes for you, but the trade off is still yours to tune. terms.title: Speculative Decoding
terms.passage:
A serving technique where a small draft model guesses several tokens ahead and the large model checks them in one pass.

Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a cheap model guess ahead and an expensive model check the guesses. A small draft model proposes the next few tokens, say four or five, and the large target model runs a single forward pass over all of them at once. Every proposed token the target agrees with is kept; at the first disagreement, the target's own choice replaces it and drafting starts again from there. It works because normal decoding wastes the hardware. Generating one token at a time is limited by how fast the GPU can read the model's weights and KV cache from memory, not by arithmetic, so checking five tokens in one pass costs little more than producing one. If the target accepts three drafted tokens on average, you get roughly three or four tokens for the price of one large model step plus some cheap draft steps. The output does not get worse. With greedy decoding the result is identical to what the target would have produced alone. terms.title: Speech-to-Text (STT)
terms.passage:
Converting spoken audio into written text, the first stage of most voice AI pipelines.

Speech to text, also called automatic speech recognition or ASR, turns audio into a transcript that downstream systems can read. In a voice agent, it is the first stage: whatever the STT model writes down is all the LLM knows about what the caller said. If recognition is wrong, the most capable model in the world will confidently answer the wrong question. Errors cluster in predictable places. Proper nouns, product names, account numbers, accents and noisy environments are the usual culprits. An insurance claims line kept hearing the policy prefix "QX" as "Q ex" or "queue X", so lookups failed and the agent told callers their policy did not exist. Adding custom vocabulary hints for the prefix and validating the recognized number against the expected format cut failed lookups by more than half. Two modes matter for production. Batch transcription processes a complete recording and is accurate and cheap, which suits call analytics and meeting notes. Streaming transcription emits partial results as the person speaks, which is essential for live conversation but noisier: early partials get revised as more audio arrives. Voice agents generally act only on final segments, though some speculatively start work on partials to save time. terms.title: Streaming
terms.passage:
Sending a model's output to the client token by token as it is generated, rather than waiting for the full response.

Streaming is returning model output incrementally while it is still being generated. Instead of one HTTP response after the model finishes, the server sends a sequence of small chunks, usually over server sent events, and the client renders them as they arrive. Most LLM APIs support it with a single flag. The main benefit is perceived speed. Total generation time does not change, but the user sees the first words after the time to first token rather than after the full response. For a reply that takes eight seconds to complete, that can be the difference between a user waiting and a user leaving. Chat products almost always stream for this reason. Streaming adds engineering work in places teams do not expect. Proxies and load balancers sometimes buffer responses, so streaming works locally and then arrives all at once in production. One team spent two days on exactly that before finding a gateway setting that held responses until they completed. Error handling also changes: a request can start successfully and fail halfway, so the client needs a way to show a partial answer and offer a retry, and your retries and timeouts logic must treat a stalled stream differently from a failed request. terms.title: Structured Output
terms.passage:
Getting a model to return data in a fixed machine-readable shape, such as JSON matching a schema, instead of free text.

Structured output means constraining a model to produce data your code can parse reliably, usually JSON that matches a defined schema. Instead of asking for a paragraph and scraping it with regular expressions, you specify the fields, types and allowed values, and the model fills them in. Many APIs now support this natively, either through a JSON mode or by enforcing a schema during generation. The need becomes obvious the first time a parser breaks in production. One team's order extraction service worked in testing, then started throwing exceptions on about 2 percent of real emails. The model sometimes wrapped the JSON in a markdown code fence, sometimes added a friendly sentence before it, and occasionally returned "quantity": "two" instead of a number. Switching to schema enforced output removed the parse failures entirely. Valid shape is not the same as correct content. A schema guarantees that "refund amount" is a number; it does not guarantee the number is right. Models under a strict schema can still invent values to fill required fields, which is a quiet form of hallucination. Make fields optional or nullable when the information may be missing, add an explicit "unknown" option to enums, and check accuracy with evals rather than trusting that parsing succeeded. terms.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
terms.passage:
Training a pretrained model on prompt and ideal-response pairs so it learns to imitate those responses.

Supervised fine tuning (SFT) trains a pretrained model on examples of a prompt paired with the response you want, adjusting its weights so it produces similar responses to similar prompts. It is the most common form of fine tuning, and it is also the stage that turns a raw pretrained LLM into an instruction following assistant before any preference training. SFT teaches imitation, and the model imitates everything in the data. A team fine tuned a small model on 2,000 real support transcripts and found it reproduced agents' typos, their habit of saying "let me check that for you" with nothing to check, and order numbers that looked plausible but did not exist. The human agents had looked those numbers up in a tool the model never saw, so the model learned to produce the shape of an order number without the lookup. That is a training data cause of hallucination. The training objective is next token prediction on the target response. Each example is formatted with the same chat template the model will see at inference time, and the loss is usually computed only on the response tokens, so the model learns to answer rather than to reproduce prompts. terms.title: System Prompt
terms.passage:
The standing instructions placed before a conversation that set a model's role, rules, tone and output format for every turn.

A system prompt is a block of instructions that sits at the start of every request and frames how the model should behave. It typically defines the assistant's role, the rules it must follow, the tone, the output format and how to handle edge cases. Most chat APIs give it a dedicated slot separate from user messages, and models are trained to give it more weight. The system prompt is where product decisions become model behavior. If the bot must never discuss pricing, always answer in the user's language, or refuse to give medical advice, those rules start here. One retail team discovered their assistant was happily recommending competitors' products because nothing in the system prompt told it otherwise. A single line fixed it, but only after a screenshot circulated internally. It is not a security boundary. Users can often get a model to reveal or ignore its system prompt through jailbreak attempts or prompt injection hidden in documents. Do not put secrets, API keys or internal URLs in it, and do not rely on it alone to block harmful actions. Enforce critical rules in code with guardrails and permission checks. terms.title: Temperature
terms.passage:
A sampling setting that controls how random a model's word choices are; low values are focused, high values more varied.

Temperature is a parameter that controls how much randomness goes into choosing each next token. At every step the model produces a probability for every possible next token. Temperature reshapes that distribution before sampling: low values sharpen it so the most likely token almost always wins, high values flatten it so less likely tokens get picked more often. The practical effect is a dial between consistency and variety. Near zero, the same prompt tends to give the same answer, which suits extraction, classification and structured output. Around 0.7 to 1.0, outputs vary more, which can help brainstorming or creative copy. Much above 1.0, text becomes erratic quickly. One team had an extraction pipeline that failed to return valid JSON about one time in forty. The prompt was fine; temperature had been left at the SDK default of 1.0. Dropping it to 0 removed most failures and made their evals stable enough to compare prompt versions meaningfully. Low temperature does not make a model correct. It makes it consistent, which includes being consistently wrong. It also does not guarantee

terms.title: Text-to-Speech (TTS)
terms.passage:
Generating spoken audio from text, giving an AI system a voice for calls, assistants and accessibility.

Text to speech converts written text into synthetic audio. In a voice agent, it is the final stage, turning the LLM's reply into something the caller hears. Modern neural TTS can sound close to human, with control over voice, speed and sometimes emotion, but the quality users perceive depends heavily on what text you feed it and how quickly it starts speaking. Time to first audio matters more than total synthesis time. Users judge responsiveness by when the voice begins, not when the sentence ends. The common approach is to stream the LLM's output, split it at sentence or clause boundaries, and send each piece to TTS as soon as it is ready, so speech begins while the model is still writing. This mirrors the role of time to first token in text interfaces. The most common production problems come from text that reads fine but sounds wrong. A pharmacy assistant's replies included "Take 2.5mg 2x/day", which the TTS engine pronounced as "two point five M G two X slash day". Callers were confused and some called back to check. The fix was a normalization step that rewrote units, abbreviations, dates and symbols into speakable words before synthesis, plus a system prompt change telling the model to write for the ear. terms.title: Throughput
terms.passage:
How much work a model deployment completes per unit of time, measured in tokens or requests per second across all users.

Throughput is the total amount of work a system completes over time, usually measured in output tokens per second or requests per second across all concurrent users. It is a property of the whole deployment, not of a single request. Latency tells you how long one user waits; throughput tells you how many users you can serve at once with acceptable waits. The two are easy to confuse until load arrives. A team benchmarked their self hosted model by sending one request at a time, measured 80 tokens per second, and sized hardware assuming that number would scale linearly with GPUs. In production, with 50 concurrent users, each user saw about 15 tokens per second while total throughput was far higher than the benchmark suggested. Their capacity estimate was wrong in both directions: they had overestimated per user speed and underestimated total capacity. Several factors set the throughput of an LLM deployment. Batching is the largest lever, because GPUs are much more efficient when processing many sequences together. Memory limits how many sequences fit at once, which ties throughput to KV cache size, context length, and quantization. Output length matters too: generating tokens is slower per token than processing the prompt, so a workload of long answers needs far more capacity than one of short classifications. terms.title: Time to First Token (TTFT)
terms.passage:
The delay between sending a request and receiving the first generated token, which sets how responsive an AI feature feels.

Time to first token is how long it takes from sending a request until the model emits its first piece of output. It covers network time, queueing at the provider, and the prefill phase of inference, where the model reads the entire prompt before it can write anything. When responses are streamed, TTFT is the moment the user stops staring at a spinner. TTFT is the metric users feel most directly in chat interfaces. A reply that starts after 400 milliseconds and takes six seconds to finish usually feels faster than one that appears all at once after four seconds. That is why it deserves its own dashboard panel, separate from total latency. The biggest driver you control is prompt length. Prefill time grows with the number of input tokens, so every retrieved document, tool definition and line of conversation history adds delay before the first word. One team watched TTFT creep from under a second to nearly four over a quarter. Nothing was broken; the system prompt had grown with each incident fix, retrieval had gone from three chunks to twelve, and long chats were sending full history on every turn. terms.title: Tokenizer
terms.passage:
The component that splits text into the token IDs a model reads, usually learned with byte-pair encoding over a training corpus.

A tokenizer converts text into the sequence of integer IDs a model actually processes, and converts the model's output IDs back into text. It is fixed when the model is trained, so every LLM family ships with its own, and the same sentence can become a different number of tokens depending on which model you call. Most current tokenizers use byte pair encoding (BPE) or a close relative. Training starts from individual bytes or characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, until the vocabulary reaches a target size, commonly from about 32,000 to over 200,000 entries. Common words end up as single tokens, rarer words split into pieces, and in byte level tokenizers anything unusual falls back to individual bytes, so no input is ever unrepresentable. The merge rules reflect the training data, which produces uneven costs. A team that budgeted from English traffic found their Thai and Hindi users cost two to three times more per message, because those scripts were less common in the tokenizer's corpus and broke into many more tokens per word. The same effect hits code, long numbers and unusual whitespace. When they switched model families, their cost forecast was off by about 30 percent because they had kept counting with the old tokenizer. Input Typical behaviour Common English

terms.title: Tokens
terms.passage:
The chunks of text a language model actually reads and writes, and the unit you are billed and rate-limited by.

Tokens are the units of text a language model processes. A tokenizer splits input into pieces that are often whole common words, fragments of rarer words, punctuation or whitespace. As a rough rule, one token is about four characters of English, but code, numbers and non English text usually take more tokens per character. Tokens matter because almost every limit and cost in an LLM system is measured in them. The context window is a token budget. Provider pricing is per million input and output tokens, with output usually priced several times higher. Rate limits are often expressed as tokens per minute. If you only think in characters or words, your estimates will drift. A common production surprise is the bill that jumps without any change in traffic. One team saw costs triple in a month and traced it to a feature that pasted full JSON API responses into the prompt. The payloads were full of repeated keys, quotes and braces, all of which tokenize poorly. Trimming the fields and reformatting the data as compact text cut input tokens by about 70 percent. Proper cost tracking per feature would have caught it in days rather than weeks. Output tokens deserve separate attention because they drive both cost and latency. terms.title: Tool Calling
terms.passage:
A model capability where it returns a structured request to run a named function with arguments, which your code then executes.

Tool calling is the capability that lets a model respond with a structured request to run a specific function, with specific arguments, instead of plain text. Your application executes the function, sends the result back to the model, and the model continues with that new information. The model never runs anything itself; it only asks. This is what connects a model to live data and actions. Without it, an assistant asked "where is my order?" can only guess or apologize. With a get order status tool, it emits a call like {"name": "get order status", "arguments": {"order id": "A1923"}} , your code queries the database, and the model answers from the real status. It is the mechanism underneath every agent. The round trip has a consistent shape. You send the conversation along with a list of available tools, each described by a function schema. The model either replies normally or returns one or more tool calls. You validate the arguments, run the functions, append the results to the conversation, and call the model again. Many models can request several independent calls at once, which you can execute in parallel to save time. Most production bugs with tool calling come from the model choosing badly, not from the API. terms.title: Top-p Sampling
terms.passage:
A sampling method that limits each next-token choice to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.

Top p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, restricts which tokens the model is allowed to pick at each step. The model ranks every candidate token by probability, then keeps only the top ones until their combined probability reaches the threshold p. Sampling happens within that shortlist. With p set to 0.9, the long tail of unlikely tokens making up the last 10 percent is discarded. The point is to cut off nonsense without forcing the model to always take the single most likely word. When the model is confident, the nucleus might contain one or two tokens; when it is uncertain, it might contain dozens. That adaptive behavior is what distinguishes top p from top k, which keeps a fixed number of candidates regardless of confidence. Top p and temperature both control randomness, and changing both at once makes behavior hard to reason about. Temperature reshapes the probabilities; top p then trims the list. A team debugging odd word choices in generated product descriptions found that someone had set temperature to 1.3 and top p to 0.5 in an attempt to make copy "creative but safe". The two settings fought each other, producing text that was oddly repetitive in some places and bizarre in others. Resetting top p to 1.0 and tuning only temperature gave predictable results. terms.title: Tracing
terms.passage:
Recording every step behind one LLM request, such as model calls, retrievals and tool calls, as a timed tree of spans.

Tracing captures everything that happened while serving one request as a connected tree of spans. The root span is the user's request; child spans are each model call, retrieval, reranking step, tool call and guardrail check it triggered, each with its own start time, duration, inputs, outputs and metadata like token counts. It is the most useful single tool in LLM observability. Its value is clearest in multi step systems. An agent that answers a question by calling search three times, reading two documents and calling a calculator generates a dozen operations. When the final answer is wrong, a flat log shows you a pile of unrelated lines. A trace shows you the sequence: which search query the model wrote, what came back, and where the reasoning went off course. Tracing is also how you find latency problems. A team noticed their assistant's p95 latency had climbed from four seconds to eleven. Aggregate metrics only told them it was slow. Opening a few slow traces showed the agent loop occasionally calling the same lookup tool five or six times in a row because a tool error message was ambiguous. terms.title: Transformer
terms.passage:
The neural network architecture behind modern LLMs, built around attention so every token can weigh every earlier token.

A transformer is the neural network architecture almost every modern LLM is built on. It processes a sequence of tokens through a stack of identical layers, and each layer has two main parts: an attention block that lets each token gather information from other tokens, and a feed forward block that transforms each token's representation on its own. Attention is the idea that makes the architecture work. For every token, the layer computes three vectors: a query, a key and a value. It scores the token's query against the keys of the other tokens, turns those scores into weights with a softmax, and takes a weighted sum of their values. A model generating text uses causal attention, so each token can only look at tokens before it. Many attention "heads" run in parallel, each free to learn a different kind of relationship, such as which noun a pronoun refers to. The architecture explains several symptoms engineers see in production. One team found that doubling their prompt length made the first token arrive more than twice as late. Attention compares every token with every earlier token, so its share of the prompt processing work grows with the square of the prompt length. terms.title: Turn Detection
terms.passage:
Deciding when a speaker has finished their turn so a voice agent knows when to respond and when to keep listening.

Turn detection, sometimes called endpointing, is how a voice agent decides that the person has finished speaking and it is time to reply. Humans do this effortlessly using pauses, intonation, grammar and context. Machines have to infer it from an audio stream and partial transcripts, and getting it wrong is one of the most noticeable failures in voice products. There are two ways to fail, and they pull in opposite directions. Respond too early and the agent cuts people off mid sentence, especially when they pause to think or recall a number. Respond too late and every exchange carries dead air that adds directly to latency. A bank's voice line used a fixed 500 millisecond silence threshold. Callers reading out sixteen digit card numbers naturally paused between groups of four, and the agent kept jumping in after the first group with "Sorry, that doesn't look like a valid card number." terms.title: User Feedback Loops
terms.passage:
Collecting signals from real users, explicit ratings and implicit behavior, and feeding them back into evals, prompts and data.

A user feedback loop is the process of capturing what real users think of a model's output, in what they say and in what they do, and feeding that back into how the system is built. The loop only counts as closed when a signal from production ends up changing something: an eval case, a prompt, a retrieval fix or training data. Explicit feedback alone is usually too thin to steer by. One team shipped a thumbs up/down button and got ratings on under one percent of conversations, almost all thumbs down from frustrated users. The useful signal was in behavior they were not logging yet: users who regenerated an answer three times, rewrote the draft before sending it, or asked for a human right after the bot replied. Once those events were tied to the tracing data for each conversation, the team could find the worst failures without waiting for anyone to click a button. terms.title: Vector Database
terms.passage:
A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the ones nearest to a query vector, often alongside metadata filters.

A vector database stores embeddings and answers the question "which stored vectors are closest to this one?" quickly, even across millions or billions of items. It builds approximate nearest neighbor indexes for similarity search, stores the original text or an ID alongside each vector, and usually supports metadata filtering so you can restrict results by tenant, date, language or document type. You do not always need a dedicated product. For a few hundred thousand vectors, a vector extension in the relational database you already run is often enough, and it keeps your data in one place with existing backups and access controls. Dedicated vector databases earn their keep at larger scale, with high query volume, or when you need features like built in hybrid search. The operational problems are mostly about keeping the index in step with the source data. One team's assistant kept quoting a pricing page that had been changed two months earlier. The documents were updated in the CMS, but the ingestion job only added new pages and never re embedded edited ones. Another team leaked one customer's documents into another's answers because the tenant filter was applied in application code that a new endpoint bypassed. terms.title: Voice Agents
terms.passage:
AI agents that hold spoken conversations in real time, combining speech recognition, an LLM and speech synthesis.

A voice agent is an agent you talk to rather than type to. It listens to audio, works out what the caller said, decides how to respond, possibly calls tools, and speaks back, all within the rhythm of a normal conversation. Phone support lines, appointment booking, drive through ordering and in car assistants are typical uses. Most voice agents are built as a pipeline: Stage Job Typical delay Speech to text Turn caller audio into text 100–300 ms Turn detection Decide the caller has finished 200–800 ms LLM Generate the reply, maybe call tools 300–1500 ms to first token Text to speech Turn reply text into audio 100–300 ms to first audio Some newer systems use speech to speech models that skip the text stages, trading control and observability for lower delay and more natural prosody. Latency is the defining constraint. In text chat, a two second wait is fine. On a phone call, anything above about a second feels like the line went dead, and callers start saying "hello?" which the system then treats as a new utterance. A clinic's booking agent had a median response time of 2.4 seconds; callers routinely talked over it, the agent restarted its answer, and conversations spiraled. terms.title: Workflows vs Agents
terms.passage:
The design choice between code that fixes the sequence of LLM calls and a model that decides its own next step at runtime.

A workflow is a system where your code decides the order of LLM calls and tools, while an agent is a system where the model decides what to do next at runtime. Both use the same parts: prompts, tool calling and structured output. The difference is who holds the control flow, and that choice shapes cost, latency and how easy the system is to test. Teams often start with an agent when a workflow would have done the job. One support team gave a model a dozen tools and the instruction "resolve the ticket". It worked in demos, but in production each ticket took eight to fifteen model calls, the p95 was over a minute, and no two runs of the same ticket looked alike. When they looked at the logs, almost every ticket followed one of five paths: refund, shipping status, password reset, bug report or escalation. Rebuilding it as a workflow (classify, route to one of five fixed handlers, draft a reply) cut cost by roughly 70 percent and made every path testable with ordinary evals.
